topic: Recursive Agent Handoffs Cascade Into Infinite Loops
postText:
Multi-agent orchestration promises self-healing workflows, but in production, unconstrained autonomous collaboration quickly degenerates into an expensive death spiral.

In healthcare IT, we piloted multi-agent pipelines to assist in reconciling messy clinical discharge summaries. Agent A parsed ambiguous physician notes, Agent B validated formulary medication records, and Agent C resolved conflicting entries. On paper, it was seamless emergent intelligence. In reality, an edge-case lab value triggered an infinite circular handoff: Agent B and Agent C endlessly debated drug interactions, repeatedly firing live DB and API calls until gateway rate limiters throttled our cluster.

Deploying LLM autonomy without classic distributed systems discipline invites silent production outages. We stabilized the swarm with three guardrails:

1. Deterministic State Machines: Replace free-form agent dialogue with directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Agents propose state updates, but orchestrator logic controls transition legality.
2. Hard Recursion Limits: Enforce absolute hop limits and token budgets per trace. If reconciliation exceeds six hops, fail fast to human review.
3. Idempotent Tool Proxies: Downstream tools must require deterministic idempotency keys generated from conversation state, preventing redundant execution cascades.

Without hard deterministic guardrails, multi-agent autonomy is just an accidental denial-of-service attack waiting to execute on your internal microservices.

How do you govern multi-agent autonomy in your stack: strict deterministic state graphs or dynamic LLM-driven evaluators?
